subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Aparna, and I sit next to Akash. During the science test he kept scratching his head and rubbing his forehead. I guessed he was stuck, and I felt bad for him. After the test I asked, “Were you stuck?” He laughed. “Not really. My cap made my head itch, and I was sleepy because of the late cricket match. But I was stuck on question five.” So I was partly right and partly wrong. Next time I'll just whisper, “Do you need anything?” without guessing first.

qa.q: What did Akash keep doing during the science test?
qa.a: Akash kept scratching his head and rubbing his forehead.

qa.q: What did Aparna guess Akash was feeling, and how right was that guess?
qa.a: Aparna guessed he was stuck, and was partly right, since he was stuck on question five. His itchy head and sleepiness, from his cap and the late match, also explained the scratching.

qa.q: What would you advise Aparna to do next time?
qa.a: Offer a friendly “Do you need anything?” after the test or quietly, as Aparna plans, without guessing first.

qa.q: How might Akash feel about Aparna's question?
qa.a: Probably amused and glad someone noticed. He answered honestly and laughed, so he does not seem bothered.

grounding: A peer scratching the head during a test may be stuck, itchy or tired; asking beats assuming.

Wednesday: she scratched her head again. Kamal asked after the paper, “Stuck or itchy?” “Stuck on the last one!” she laughed.
Friday: Arohi rubbed her forehead during the spelling test. Kamal just slid his eraser to the side of the desk, in case she needed it. She looked up and smiled, and kept writing.

qa.q: What did Arohi say when Kamal asked if she was stuck on Monday?
qa.a: She said, “No, just an itch.”

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on Wednesday when she scratched her head, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: She was probably stuck on the last question, as she said afterwards. On Monday the same gesture was just an itch, so the gesture alone does not tell which.

qa.q: How did Kamal's approach improve between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: He moved from guessing to asking “Stuck or itchy?”, and by Friday he offered a small helpful gesture without interrupting her writing.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel on Friday when Arohi rubs her forehead?
qa.a: Kamal probably feels caring and relaxed about it now, quietly sliding the eraser over instead of asking again.

grounding: Scratching the head may be confusion, an itch or tiredness; a friendly offer beats assuming.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: Avni, you keep rubbing your forehead; it reminds me of a boy I taught forty years ago. Your old Urmila Teacher had a pupil, Raju, who scratched his head and rubbed his forehead through every test. I decided he was always lost and kept explaining the sums to him, slowly, in front of everyone. His face got redder every time. One day I asked him quietly at my desk, “Are you stuck, or is something else going on?” He said, “I know the sums, Teacher. I'm just sleepy. My baby sister cries all night.” After that I let him sit by the window and never explained in front of the class again.

qa.q: What did Raju do through every test?
qa.a: Raju scratched his head and rubbed his forehead through every test.

qa.q: What was Raju feeling when his face got redder?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at being treated as lost in front of everyone, when he actually knew the sums.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make that changed things?
qa.a: She asked Raju quietly at her desk whether he was stuck or something else was going on, which showed he was just sleepy.

qa.q: How did young Urmila Teacher first read Raju's head-scratching?
qa.a: She first read it as confusion and kept explaining the sums, not guessing he was tired from sleepless nights.

grounding: Shows head-scratching and forehead-rubbing during tests being read as confusion when it was tiredness, and a friendly question working better.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: The exam hall was silent except for the ceiling fans, and talking meant a zero. Two rows ahead, Sarika kept scratching the side of her head and rubbing her forehead hard. Nilesh watched. She's stuck on the long question. He wanted to help but couldn't say a word. When she turned, he caught her eye and mouthed, “Okay?” She pulled a face and pointed at her forehead. After the bell, Nilesh found her at the gate. “Were you stuck on question five?” Sarika laughed. “No, I finished it. A mosquito got me three times in the night. It itched like mad.” She showed him the bumps. Nilesh grinned. “Stuck with mosquitoes, then.”

qa.q: How many times had the mosquito bitten Sarika?
qa.a: A mosquito got her three times in the night.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling as he watched Sarika rub her forehead?
qa.a: Nilesh felt concerned and helpless, thinking she was stuck on the long question and unable to help in the silent hall.

qa.q: How did Nilesh check his guess within the exam rules?
qa.a: He silently mouthed “Okay?” and then asked after the bell, instead of assuming she was stuck.

qa.q: What was the exam like for Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika knew the answers but was distracted by itchy mosquito bites, which explained the scratching.

grounding: Shows a child guessing a peer's head-scratching in a test means confusion, then asking and finding it was an itch.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage: In Sunaina's flat in Chennai, the two friends were doing maths homework at the dining table. Keerthana stopped writing, scratched her head and rubbed her forehead with the heel of her hand, again and again. Sunaina almost said, “It's easy, you just divide,” but stopped herself. She remembered how annoying it felt when her brother did that to her. Instead she asked, “Are you stuck, or just tired?” Keerthana yawned hugely. “Tired. Swimming at five-thirty this morning. I know how to do it; my brain's just slow.” Sunaina pushed the plate of murukku across. “Snack break, then. Ten minutes.”

qa.q: What time did Keerthana go swimming?
qa.a: Keerthana went swimming at five-thirty that morning.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she rubbed her forehead?
qa.a: She was tired from early swimming, not confused, though it looked as if she might be stuck.

qa.q: Why was Sunaina's question better than explaining straight away?
qa.a: Asking “stuck, or just tired?” found the real cause, so Sunaina offered a snack break instead of an unneeded explanation.

qa.q: What would change if Sunaina had jumped in with “It's easy”?
qa.a: Keerthana might have felt talked down to, since she already knew how to do it and was only tired.

grounding: Shows a child seeing a friend rub her forehead over homework and asking are you stuck instead of assuming confusion.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]

"Mahima, you've scratched your head about fifty times," Shreya whispered across their shared desk.
"Have I?"
"And now you're rubbing your forehead. Stuck on the worksheet?"
"Not stuck. Itchy! Amma oiled my hair last night, and now my whole head's crawling."
"Eww. Okay."
"And I slept really late because of my cousin's wedding. My brain feels like cotton."
"So not confused, just itchy and tired?"
Mahima looked at the page again. "Well… number six is a bit confusing."
"Want to do it together?"
"Yes, please. But don't lean on my oily head."

qa.q: What had Amma done the night before?
qa.a: Amma oiled Mahima's hair last night.

qa.q: Why did Mahima keep scratching and rubbing her forehead?
qa.a: Mostly because her oiled head itched and she felt tired after a late night; only a little because she felt confused by number six.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that worked better than guessing?
qa.a: She asked a friendly "Stuck on the worksheet?", which uncovered the real reasons and still led to help with number six.

qa.q: What would change if Shreya had told the teacher that Mahima didn't understand anything?
qa.a: Mahima would feel embarrassed and misjudged, since the scratching was mostly itching and tiredness.

grounding: It shows a child seeing a partner scratch her head and rub her forehead, and a friendly are-you-stuck question revealing an itch and tiredness.
